subject: radiology
title: Radiographic Technique: Kilovoltage, Tube Current, and Filtration

steps.title: Tube Potential and Penetration
steps.tx: **Peak kilovoltage penetration** governs the maximum kinetic energy imparted to electrons traversing the vacuum gap. Because beam quality reflects the penetrating capability of X-ray photons, raising the tube potential enables the beam to pass through dense osseous and muscular structures. Higher kilovoltages favour Compton scatter over photoelectric absorption, diminishing subject contrast while broadening the exposure latitude on the final radiograph.

left.title: Low Kilovoltage Settings (50-65 kVp)
points: High contrast with stark black and white boundaries
Restricted to thin extremities and mammography

right.title: High Kilovoltage Settings (100-140 kVp)
points: Long greyscale latitude with subtle gradations
Standard for chest radiography to visualize lung parenchyma

steps.tx: An **X-ray emission spectrum** plots how many photons leave the tube at each energy. Raising peak kilovoltage moves the bremsstrahlung curve to the right and raises its height, so the beam is harder and more intense together. Raising milliampere seconds multiplies every point on that curve by the same factor and leaves the maximum energy where it was. The two controls therefore separate quality from quantity. A spectrum drawn at two kilovoltage settings and two milliampere second settings makes that split visible at a glance.
steps.say: An emission spectrum shows that higher kilovoltage hardens the beam and lifts output, while milliampere seconds only change how many photons are produced.

vis.alt: X-ray emission spectra comparing the effect of changing kilovoltage and tube current
vis.caption: Emission spectra compare a higher kilovoltage, which hardens and intensifies the beam, with a higher milliampere second setting, which raises photon number only. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: Tube Current and Exposure Quantity
steps.tx: **Milliampere-second exposure control** determines the total number of X-ray photons produced during an examination without altering photon energy. Tube current, measured in milliamperes, reflects the rate of electron flow across the tube. Multiplying milliamperes by exposure time in seconds gives milliampere-seconds. Doubling milliampere-seconds doubles the number of photons striking the detector, directly controlling optical density.

steps.title: The Fifteen Percent Rule
steps.tx: **Fifteen percent kilovoltage rule** guides exposure adjustments in clinical practice. Increasing the peak tube potential by 15 percent doubles the effective exposure reaching the radiographic image receptor, yielding an effect identical to doubling the milliampere-seconds. Radiographers exploit this relationship by raising kilovoltage by 15 percent while halving milliampere-seconds, substantially reducing patient entrance skin dose.

steps.title: Inherent Tube Filtration
steps.tx: **Inherent tube filtration** refers to the permanent structural materials through which the emerging X-ray beam must pass before exiting the housing. These components include the glass or metal vacuum tube wall, the surrounding insulating dielectric oil bath, and the radiolucent exit port window. Together, these elements provide roughly 0.5 to 1.0 millimetres of aluminium equivalent filtration.

steps.title: Added Aluminium Filtration
steps.tx: **Added aluminium filtration** consists of dedicated metal sheets inserted between the tube housing and the collimator aperture. Low-energy photons below 20 kiloelectron volts have insufficient energy to penetrate human tissues, contributing zero diagnostic information while depositing unwanted radiation into superficial skin layers. Added aluminium preferentially attenuates these non-penetrating photons, shifting the mean energy upward in a process termed beam hardening.

left.title: Unfiltered Polyenergetic Beam
points: Contains high flux of soft 10 to 25 keV photons
Entirely absorbed within patient epidermis and dermis
Elevates entrance skin dose without reaching detector

right.title: Filtered Hardened Beam
points: Soft low-energy photons attenuated by aluminium
Mean photon energy shifts toward higher penetrating values
Decreases patient dose while preserving contrast

steps.tx: The softest photons in the beam can only harm, so they are removed before the patient. **Beam filtration** with aluminium absorbs low energy photons that would stop in skin and contribute dose without reaching the receptor. The beam that survives is harder, with a higher average energy and better penetration per unit of skin dose. Inherent and added filtration together are specified and tested because this invisible metal sheet is a safety device.
steps.say: Aluminium filtration removes low energy photons that only dose skin. The surviving harder beam images with less surface dose.

vis.alt: Diagram of X-ray beam filtration, aluminium absorbing low energy soft photons.
vis.caption: Soft photons stop in an aluminium sheet while harder photons pass through. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: Total Filtration Regulatory Standards
steps.tx: **Total filtration requirements** are mandated by international radiation protection bodies to guarantee clinical safety. Total filtration represents the numerical sum of inherent and added filtration. Diagnostic X-ray equipment operating above 70 peak kilovolts must maintain a minimum total filtration of 2.5 millimetres of aluminium equivalent, whereas machines operating between 50 and 70 kilovolts require at least 1.5 millimetres.

steps.title: Half-Value Layer Measurement
steps.tx: **Half-value layer measurement** provides the most accurate experimental index of X-ray beam quality and penetrability. It is defined as the thickness of a specified absorbing material, typically aluminium, required to reduce beam exposure rate by exactly 50 percent. When an X-ray unit fails its statutory half-value layer test, insufficient filtration or an inaccurate kilovoltage generator calibration is suspected.

steps.title: Optimizing Patient Entrance Dose
steps.tx: **Entrance skin dose optimization** relies on balancing kilovoltage and tube current during radiographic setup. Choosing higher tube potentials paired with reduced milliampere-seconds lowers the radiation absorbed by the patient's skin and superficial tissues. Because higher-energy photons penetrate through the patient with greater probability, fewer total photons need to be fired from the tube to produce an identical detector signal.
